AI-Assisted Programming and Labor Demand∗

Lindsey Raymond Eleanor Dillon
MIT Microsoft Research

November 6, 2026

JEL Classifications: J23, J24, J63, M15, M51, O33
Keywords: Generative AI, Large Language Models, Technology Adoption, Labor Demand, Hiring, Software Engineering, Entry-Level Workers, Human Capital.

 

∗Correspondence to lraymond@mit.edu and eleanor.dillon@microsoft.com. We are enormously grateful to Lisa Simon, Brian Xu, Kevin Xu, and Ben Zweig for invaluable data assistance, to Bee Xiong for helpful conversations about the GitHub sales process. Abstract

Generative AI has demonstrated human-level performance on technical work tasks, yet evidence on how these task-level capabilities are changing labor demand remains scarce. We study the firm-level adoption of GitHub Copilot, an AI coding assistant, across 5,414 multinational firms accounting for 38% of the U.S. programming workforce. To identify causal effects, we exploit a natural experiment generated by firms’ predetermined software procurement cycles. Early AI-adopting firms hired more workers before the launch of GitHub Copilot and had larger, more technical, and older workforces. After one year, GitHub Copilot adoption reduces quarterly technical hiring by 29% among review-induced adopters, with no effect on separations, overall technical headcount, or vacancy duration. The hiring slowdown is concentrated in the subset of junior technical roles that involve the highest share of coding work. Overall, AI coding assistance causes firms to shift demand towards more experienced workers and roles that pair some coding with broader design responsibilities.

1   Introduction

LLMs now rival or exceed human performance on some tasks in mathematics, legal and financial analysis, and software development (Rein et al., 2023; Luong et al., 2025; Guha et al., 2023). Progress has been especially rapid in programming, where AI coding assistants can generate, explain, test, and debug code. As organizations incorporate these task-level improvements and redesign workflows, firms may reduce demand for human work that can now be done more effectively by machines while expanding opportunities for human work that complements AI. Understanding where these changes will be felt helps workers, firms, and policymakers adjust efficiently. However, the mapping from task-level technical capabilities to role- and firm-level demand changes is difficult to predict and difficult to measure. Field experiments can randomize access to AI across workers, but equivalent experiments across firms are generally infeasible. Absent randomization, firms that adopt AI early may already follow different growth trajectories or employ distinct management practices. Observational studies cannot reliably separate this endogenous choice by firms to adopt AI, other concurrent economic shocks, and the direct effects of AI on labor demand.

This paper exploits a natural experiment in firm-level AI adoption to provide causal evidence on how AI coding assistants affect hiring and employment for technical workers. While AI coding assistants are our broader object of study, we focus on GitHub Copilot because it is the setting for which we have data access and a clean empirical design. We study its rollout across 5,414 multinational firms employing 45 million workers worldwide, including 38% of the U.S. programming workforce. Our identification strategy rests on the centralized and complex nature of enterprise software procurement. In large firms, individual developers cannot independently deploy new software tools; instead, adoption must proceed through a formal procurement process involving dedicated legal, security, compliance, and purchasing personnel. All firms in our sample were GitHub customers using GitHub’s enterprise product for code management before GitHub Copilot’s January 2023 launch. These enterprise customers follow a regular schedule for contract reviews with GitHub, during which the relevant teams for coordinating contract evaluations and budgetary decisions are assembled. Firms faced a lower organizational cost of adopting GitHub Copilot during these existing GitHub reviews relative to initiating a separate procurement process. Because these schedules were established before GitHub Copilot existed, their timing provides plausibly exogenous variation in the timing of adoption, unrelated to firms’ underlying employment trajectories.

One year post-review, treated firms are 20 percentage points more likely to have adopted GitHub Copilot than not-yet-reviewed firms. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design that compares earlier- and later-reviewed firms, we estimate both the first-stage effect of review timing on GitHub Copilot adoption and its reduced-form effect on employment. Under additional assumptions, the Wald ratio of these two estimates identifies the causal effect of GitHub Copilot among firms induced to adopt earlier by the instrument of their pre-scheduled contract reviews.

We link GitHub’s administrative records on coding assistant adoption and contract reviews to employment data from Revelio Labs, which tracks firm-level headcount, hiring, and separations by role and seniority. This matched dataset allows us to observe actual enterprise AI adoption rather than relying on indirect proxies or occupational exposure scores. We focus on firms headquartered in the Americas and Europe, where GitHub’s enterprise customer base is concentrated and Revelio provides comprehensive coverage. The resulting monthly panel runs from January 2021 through June 2025, which spans two years before and two and a half years after GitHub Copilot’s January 2023 enterprise launch. Over this window, GitHub Copilot was the dominant enterprise coding assistant, predating the rollout of the enterprise versions of competing tools such as Cursor and Claude Code.

Within a firm, AI coding assistance affects labor demand through three channels: changes in the scale of software production, the allocation of tasks across roles and seniority levels, and productivity gains on existing tasks. While expanding software production raises overall labor demand, productivity gains on existing tasks reduce the labor required for a given level of output. Changes in how tasks are bundled and allocated across jobs further shape which roles and seniority levels firms require. Our empirical estimates capture the net effect of these potentially offsetting forces on employment, hiring, and separations.

Because we observe GitHub Copilot take up directly, we can cleanly identify the characteristics of early AI adopters and non-adopters. Consistent with Acemoglu et al. (2023), early AI-adopting firms in our sample hired more workers each month before the launch of GitHub Copilot. They were also larger overall with a higher share of technical workers and a lower share of junior workers. These compositional differences illustrate the econometric challenge of separating the drivers of AI adoption from the effects of adoption. Our data also highlight that generative AI tools arrived during a tumultuous period of adjustment for technical workers that affected both adopting and non-adopting firms. From January, 2022 to December, 2024, monthly mean hiring rates among firms that never adopted GitHub Copilot during our sample decreased from 2.7% to 1.8%.

Using our procurement instrument, we find that GitHub Copilot adoption reduces technical hiring without increasing separations. One year after scheduled contract review, monthly hiring for technical workers, those who build, test, deploy, secure, or support software systems, is 7.6% lower than at firms whose reviews have not yet occurred. The corresponding Wald estimates imply a 29% reduction in quarterly technical hiring among complying firms that were induced to adopt GitHub Copilot earlier by their scheduled contract reviews. From a pre-period baseline of roughly 55 quarterly technical hires per firm, the reduced-form and IV estimates imply hiring slows to about 51 and 39 workers per quarter, respectively. Against an average firm workforce of 8,000 employees, these reductions represent less than 0.2% of headcount per quarter. By contrast, we find no meaningful change in separations, suggesting that layoffs have not been a meaningful tool of adjustment for these firms. We also find no change in overall technical headcount over the first year, consistent with the small scale of the hiring changes relative to the stock of workers at these established firms.

Technical job postings also fall while posting durations remain unchanged, suggesting that the drop in hiring reflects lower labor demand rather than reduced matching efficiency. Several placebo and robustness checks weigh against the possibility that this decline is driven by corporate budgeting cycles, broader hiring freezes or AI tools adoption. Scheduled contract reviews have no effect on technical hiring prior to GitHub Copilot’s launch or post-launch hiring for non-technical professionals such as accountants, and yield similar estimates when controlling for firm-size and industry trends.

Decomposing this decline in overall technical hiring, we find GitHub Copilot reduces hiring primarily for junior workers in code-intensive roles. We measure each role’s coding intensity using pre-GitHub Copilot job descriptions and distinguish between junior and experienced workers. Neither coding intensity nor seniority alone predicts the hiring response: more code-intensive roles do not experience larger overall hiring declines, and junior hiring does not fall uniformly across all technical roles. Rather, the hiring decline is concentrated at the intersection. Four quarters after contract review, a one-standard-deviation increase in coding intensity is associated with 6.8% lower quarterly hiring among junior workers, with no comparable gradient among experienced workers. Comparing the two ends of the coding-intensity distribution illustrates this pattern: among compliers, quarterly hiring of junior software engineers falls by roughly 40%, whereas hiring of experienced software engineers and of systems and infrastructure engineers is unaffected.

This contraction in entry-level coding positions reshapes both where junior workers enter firms and the seniority mix of technical teams. Before GitHub Copilot’s launch, 72% of junior technical hires entered code-intensive roles; our estimates imply that adoption reduces this share to 52%, leaving entry-level hiring nearly evenly split between more and less code-intensive roles. This shift away from entry-level workers is striking given experimental evidence that novices realize the largest task-level productivity gains from generative AI, demonstrating that larger individual productivity effects need not translate into greater labor demand.

Although the volume of experienced software engineering hires remains stable, firms raise the bar on their qualifications and firm-specific tenure. Three to four quarters after contract review, new hires into experienced software engineering positions have roughly 1.3 additional years of potential experience and are 4.7 percentage points more likely to hold a master’s or doctoral degree. Experienced hiring also shifts toward workers with firm-specific human capital: external hires into experienced software engineering roles fall by approximately 13%, whereas internal fills remain unchanged. Among junior software engineering hires, by contrast, observable education, experience, and internal sourcing do not detectably change.

Finally, we examine whether GitHub Copilot alters the geographic distribution of hiring between firms’ home countries and India, their primary offshore engineering hub. In principle, AI coding tools could make lower-cost offshore talent more attractive by bridging time-zone and communication gaps and helping remote developers get up to speed on proprietary systems. Conversely, if offshore teams are disproportionately assigned well-defined implementation work, their roles may be more directly exposed to AI substitution. Empirically, we find no evidence that adoption shifts hiring toward India; rather, the point estimates point to a somewhat steeper slowdown in offshore hiring than at headquarters.

Together, our results show that AI coding assistance is already reshaping technical labor demand, with adjustments emerging within a year. Even within technical roles, the early impacts of AI fall unevenly, with marked decreases in hiring in the most code-intensive junior roles but no clear changes in hiring for other technical junior roles. For experienced workers, the impacts show up in the demand for specific skills rather than a change in heads hired. Two considerations are important when interpreting these findings. First, our estimates capture firm-level employment responses rather than economy-wide equilibrium effects. Reduced entry-level software engineering hiring at large adopting firms need not translate into lower aggregate technical employment, as displaced candidates may find work in other technical occupations or at smaller employers (Raymond, 2023; Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2020). Conversely, if adopting firms expand output at the expense of competitors, our estimates may capture business-stealing effects that do not translate into aggregate employment gains, potentially making market-wide effects more negative than the firm-level estimates (Acemoglu et al., 2020). Second, our estimates capture an initial adjustment period rather than a long-run steady state. As firms continue to understand the potential of AI tools, both to automate tasks and to support new work, hiring in different areas of technical work could continue to adjust in either direction.

This paper makes three contributions. First, we introduce a portable empirical strategy for identifying the firm-level causal effects of rapidly evolving technologies like enterprise AI. Because AI capabilities advance continuously across new tools and model upgrades, any single empirical study captures a specific product generation, such as our analysis of GitHub Copilot between 2023 and mid-2025. However, our identification strategy is not specific to a single tool or release. It exploits a pervasive feature of corporate software purchasing: enterprise vendors and AI providers routinely sell new products, capability upgrades, and expanded token budgets through existing customer contracts that follow predetermined review schedules. These recurring procurement cycles therefore provide a generalizable research design that researchers can use to provide causal estimates in successive waves of AI across firms, occupations, and industries.

Second, we provide the first credible causal evidence on how firm-level adoption of generative AI affects hiring, separations, and workforce composition. Existing studies report conflicting findings, documenting reduced demand for AI-exposed workers, null employment effects, or faster growth.11 1 See Brynjolfsson et al. (2025a); Humlum and Vestergaard (2025); Babina et al. (2024); Acemoglu et al. (2022); Westby et al. (2026); Chen and Stratton (2026); Yotzov et al. (2026); Fairlie and Wu (2026); Hampole et al. (2025); Chandar and Klein Teeselink (2026); Baird et al. (2026); Kharazian et al. (2026); Hosseini Maasoum and Lichtinger (2025); Tucker (2026); Klein Teeselink (2025); Daniotti et al. (2026); Dey et al. (2026); Lodefalk et al. (2026). Our analysis shows how two distinct identification challenges may explain this divergence. First, studies comparing occupations by AI exposure may risk picking up occupation-specific macroeconomic contractions, which our estimates show account for at least half of the post-2022 drop in technical hiring. Second, studies comparing adopting and non-adopting firms may face positive selection into treatment: in our sample, eventual adopters were already growing faster before our AI coding assistant launched. Our research design overcomes both challenges, separating the causal effect of adoption from firm-level selection and aggregate shocks. Combining administrative adoption records with predetermined procurement cycles overcomes both challenges to isolate the causal effect of adoption.

Third, we contribute to the literature on how technology shapes skill demand and workforce adjustment by showing how adjustment to generative AI coding assistants unfolds across hiring, separations, and skill requirements.22 2 On technology and skill demand, see Rosen (1981); Katz and Murphy (1992); Autor et al. (1998); Autor et al. (2003); Bartel et al. (2007); Goldin and Katz (2008); Michaels et al. (2014); Akerman et al. (2015); Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020); Deming and Noray (2020); Taniguchi and Yamada (2022); Autor and Thompson (2025); on technology and the organization of work inside firms, see Brynjolfsson and Hitt (2000); Athey and Stern (2002); Bresnahan et al. Firms can reduce labor input by slowing hiring or increasing separations, with the margin of adjustment varying across technologies and institutions (Abowd et al., 1999; Davis et al., 2012; Carlsson et al., 2021). Whereas industrial automation in the Netherlands displaced incumbent workers, robot adoption in Germany shifted the burden of adjustment onto young labor market entrants (Bessen et al., 2025; Dauth et al., 2021; Feigenbaum and Gross, 2024). We find that firms’ initial response to generative AI more closely resembles the latter pattern: firms reduce external hiring of early-career workers without increasing separations or reducing internal transfers. On the skill margin, our findings show that even when generative AI boosts novice productivity on individual tasks, firm-level labor demand shifts away from entry-level implementation work and toward experienced workers with advanced degrees, greater industry experience, and firm-specific human capital.

2   Setting: GitHub Copilot for Enterprise

2.1   GitHub Enterprise

Commercial software development requires large teams of engineers to collaborate on shared, interdependent codebases. When an engineer writes code to update a product feature or internal system, that change cannot simply be released to users immediately. To prevent outages and security breaches, proposed code must first be reviewed by peers, run through automated tests to ensure it works with existing systems, scanned for security vulnerabilities, and approved for release. Large organizations must also satisfy strict security and regulatory standards by controlling which employees can modify live systems, maintaining audit logs of every change, and governing the geographic region where software code is stored and accessed.

GitHub Enterprise, owned by Microsoft and used by 90% of Fortune 100 companies, is the leading platform for managing this workflow at scale (GitHub, 2026b; Wessel et al., 2023; GitHub, 2026a). Importantly, GitHub Enterprise, which we refer to as GitHub, is not an AI tool. Rather, it is the platform firms use to store their code, collaborate on software development, review changes, and manage who has access to it. Focusing on pre-existing GitHub customers therefore isolates established employers with substantial software engineering operations.

2.2   GitHub Copilot

GitHub Copilot for Enterprise is an AI coding assistant powered by large language models (LLMs) that operates directly within a developer’s code editor.33 3 For the remainder of the paper, we refer to GitHub Copilot for Enterprise as “GitHub Copilot” to differentiate the coding assistant launched for enterprises in 2023 from other Microsoft Copilot AI tools and other versions of the coding assistant designed for individuals. Appendix Section A.2 provides a brief history of ML-based coding assistants. Initially powered by OpenAI’s Codex, GitHub Copilot later integrated other frontier or customer-specific LLMs (Zhao, 2023; Zhao, 2024; Dohmke, 2024). GitHub Copilot offered two main features during our study period. In-line completion draws on surrounding code and comments to suggest single lines, entire functions, or unit tests, reducing the need to write boilerplate code or look up syntax (Panel A of Appendix Figure A.2). The chat window provides a natural-language interface to the codebase for understanding the existing codebase, looking up business logic and debugging errors (Panel B). The fact that both types of assistance appear in the same application also reduces the need to switch applications to search documentation, or use email or Slack messages to ask questions, limiting performance losses from task switching (Gonçalves et al., 2011; Meyer et al., 2017; Leroy, 2009; Kumar et al., 2025).

From its January 2023 launch through mid-2025, GitHub Copilot faced little competition in the enterprise market (Nadella, 2025). In Stack Overflow’s 2023 Developer Survey, 56.0% of respondents regularly used GitHub Copilot, compared with 4.9% for the main enterprise alternative, Amazon CodeWhisperer (Stack Overflow, 2023; Wiggers, 2024). Other prominent competitors launched enterprise tiers only after our sample period ended, including Anthropic’s Claude Code in August 2025 and Cursor in October 2025 (Anthropic, 2025; Cursor, 2025). Observing GitHub Copilot licensing captures the primary margin of enterprise AI coding adoption during our study window, limiting the concern that non-adopting firms were adopting other enterprise AI coding assistants. Even if present, unmeasured adoption in the control group would attenuate our estimates toward zero. Panel A of Figure 1 shows that sample GitHub Copilot adoption rose gradually after January 2023, reaching 62% by mid-2025. Once firms adopt, they generally provision licenses across most of their technical workforce rather than restricting access to a small number of developers.

2.3   Enterprise Procurement Cycles and Contract Review

In large firms, individual developers and managers cannot simply download and use new software tools on their own. Because enterprise software often interacts with proprietary systems and sensitive corporate data, companies block employees from installing unapproved software applications on work computers (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2018; Weill and Ross, 2004). Instead, adopting a new tool must go through a centralized procurement process: legal, security, and procurement teams must vet the vendor, verify that proprietary code and customer data are protected, and negotiate contract terms and pricing. Initiating this process outside of regular purchasing cycles requires incurring organizational frictions and coordination costs. A scheduled contract review already coordinates the legal, security, and finance teams for a planned evaluation. By contrast, an off-cycle purchase requires managers to assemble a separate business justification, wait in legal and security review queues, secure budgetary approval, and schedule meetings with all the relevant decision-makers.

Our identification strategy exploits recurring, pre-scheduled contract reviews built into firms’ existing contracts for GitHub’s source code software product. During these check-ins, a firm’s procurement team and GitHub’s sales representatives meet to adjust license counts, evaluate new features, and update contract terms. Even before GitHub Copilot’s release, account adjustments were heavily concentrated around these dates. In the pre-period, the share of firms increasing their core GitHub licenses quadrupled from roughly 10% to 40% in the two months surrounding a review, while the share reducing licenses rose from 4% to 14% (Appendix Figure A.5).44 4 While firms adjust license counts in both directions, complete platform exits are extremely rare. This concentration shows that enterprise software procurement is sticky. Even for routine license adjustments on an existing product, whether adding seats or cutting unused ones, firm modifications cluster around scheduled review windows. A natural concern is that these contract reviews coincide with firms’ broader budgeting and hiring cycles. However, as we show in Section 6.1.3, scheduled reviews prior to GitHub Copilot’s launch had no effect on technical hiring or separations (Appendix Table A.17).

Because review dates were set before GitHub Copilot’s launch, they could generate variation in when firms adopt that is plausibly unrelated to their underlying employment trajectories. We therefore use each firm’s first scheduled post-launch contract review, as recorded in December 2022, as an instrument for GitHub Copilot adoption.55 5 We use only the first post-launch review because subsequent review dates could be affected by earlier adoption decisions. Because these scheduled reviews are staggered across the calendar year rather than bunched in a single quarter, firms reach their first post-launch evaluation in different months, allowing us to compare firms arriving at a review to not-yet-reviewed firms at the same point in calendar time (Panel B of Figure 1).

While procurement stickiness clearly concentrates adjustments to core GitHub licenses around review dates, how contract reviews shape the timing and speed of GitHub Copilot adoption is an empirical question. On one hand, reaching a pre-scheduled review substantially lowered the administrative friction of adopting the tool compared to initiating an off-cycle procurement process. Because introducing a new product like GitHub Copilot is more complex than adjusting seat counts for an already integrated product, these administrative frictions could be even more binding. On the other hand, strong demand for generative AI might lead firms to adopt GitHub Copilot immediately, although the slow path of adoption in Panel A of Figure 1 weighs against this. We examine this in our first-stage analysis in Section 4.3.

3   Data

Our analysis combines three data sources: GitHub licensing data, GitHub customer relationship management (CRM) data, and Revelio Labs employment data.

3.1   GitHub Data

The GitHub data consist of monthly firm-level snapshots from January 2021 through November 2025 linked via internal identifiers. The licensing records report the number of GitHub and GitHub Copilot licenses held by each firm. We define GitHub Copilot adoption as the first month a firm holds a positive number of GitHub Copilot licenses and treat adoption as an absorbing state. To avoid endogenous sample entry, we restrict the sample to active GitHub customers as of September 2022. We obtain each firm’s first post-launch contract review date from the CRM records as of December 2022, one month prior to GitHub Copilot’s January 2023 launch.

3.2   Revelio Labs Employment Data

We measure employment stocks and flows using Revelio Labs, which aggregates public professional profiles and online job postings into standardized worker-employer histories. From individual employment spells and educational records, we construct monthly firm-level counts of headcount, new hires, and separations, both overall and by role-by-seniority cell, alongside monthly counts and average durations of job postings. Because Revelio draws primarily on LinkedIn profiles, coverage is strongest among large firms and technical workers in North America and Europe (Baird et al., 2026). We therefore restrict our sample to private-sector firms headquartered in the Americas and Europe (see Appendix Section B for details on variable construction and coverage).

3.3   Sample Characteristics

We link GitHub customers to Revelio using automated name matching supplemented by AI-assisted LinkedIn searches and human review, applying pre-2023 quality filters to exclude false matches and firms with thin profile coverage (Appendix Sections B.3–B.7 and Appendix Table A.3). The resulting balanced panel tracks 5,414 firms monthly from January 2021 through June 2025. Benchmarking Revelio against external records confirms strong alignment: total headcount correlates closely with Compustat 10-K employment in log levels (r=0.756r=0.756) and annual log changes (r=0.576r=0.576), while pre-launch software engineering headcount correlates strongly with purchased GitHub licenses in log levels (r=0.684r=0.684; Appendix Section B).

Sample firms are large, established employers: at the September 2022 baseline (Appendix Table A.4), the average firm is 47 years old and employs 8,284 workers globally, with 61.6% headquartered in the United States and the largest concentrations in information technology (24.8%) and financial services (12.9%). We classify eight roles as technical: software, data, quality-assurance, infrastructure, systems, cybersecurity, and design engineers, alongside application developers. Technical roles represent 12.6% of sample employment (5.7% in software engineering alone) and 1.6 million U.S. workers, covering 38% of the U.S. programming workforce (Appendix Section B.9 and Appendix Table A.5).66 6 As a benchmark, computer and mathematical occupations represent 3.4% of U.S. employment (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025).

4   Empirical Strategy

4.1   Technical Labor-Market Trends and Pre-Adoption Differences

Simple comparisons between GitHub Copilot adopters and non-adopters face two empirical challenges. GitHub Copilot launched during a sharp macroeconomic contraction in technical labor demand. Panel A of Figure 2 plots the mean monthly technical hiring rate (new technical hires divided by lagged technical headcount). After rising from 2.5% to 3.0% in 2021, technical hiring began falling in March 2022, ten months before GitHub Copilot’s enterprise release, coinciding with the Federal Reserve’s rapid monetary tightening cycle (Iscenko and Millet, 2026). Eventual adopters and non-adopters followed different trajectories in the pre-period. First, eventual adopters experienced a much steeper hiring surge in 2021 and contraction throughout 2022 (Panel B). Second, eventual adopters employed a higher share of technical workers, may have been differentially exposed to the broader tech slowdown, and may not have followed parallel trends with non-adopters. As a result, standard observational benchmarks could fail in two distinct ways: centering on firm adoption dates may confound treatment with pre-existing firm growth trends (Panels C and D), whereas comparing adopters with non-adopters around late 2022 may reflect differential exposure to the broader tech cycle (Panels E and F).

We first examine the adoption-centered benchmark by estimating a two-way fixed effects event study around each firm’s observed adoption month AiA_{i}:
