Standard observational regressions can therefore imply either that AI reduces employment (when measured using hiring flows) or increases employment (when measured using headcount stocks).

4.2   Instrumented Differences-in-Differences with Staggered Timing

To isolate exogenous variation in adoption timing, we instrument for GitHub Copilot adoption using the timing of each firm’s first scheduled GitHub contract review after GitHub Copilot’s launch (RiR_{i}). Let ℓ=t−Ri\ell=t-R_{i} index event time relative to this first scheduled review. We estimate the first-stage effect of reaching a contract review on GitHub Copilot adoption and the reduced-form effect on employment outcomes using the following event-study specifications:

Di​t=αi+λt+∑ℓ∈ℒπℓ𝟏{t−Ri=ℓ}+εi​tD_{it}=\alpha_{i}+\lambda_{t}+\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\pi_{\ell}\mathbf{1}\{t-R_{i}=\ell\}+\varepsilon_{it} (3)
Yi​t=αi+λt+∑ℓ∈ℒρℓ𝟏{t−Ri=ℓ}+ui​tY_{it}=\alpha_{i}+\lambda_{t}+\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\rho_{\ell}\mathbf{1}\{t-R_{i}=\ell\}+u_{it} (4)

where Di​tD_{it} is an absorbing indicator equal to one once firm ii holds a positive number of GitHub Copilot licenses and Yi​tY_{it} is an employment outcome such as headcount, hiring, or separations. For hiring and separations, which may be zero in a firm-month, we separately examine the extensive margin, an indicator for a positive value, and the intensive margin, the log outcome conditional on a positive value (Chen and Roth, 2024). We estimate firm-wide and broad occupational specifications on a balanced monthly panel; for more disaggregated role-by-seniority and within-firm analyses, where monthly hiring in individual cells is sparser, we aggregate the data to the quarterly level.

In both equations, firm fixed effects αi\alpha_{i} absorb time-invariant firm differences such as baseline size and industry, while calendar-period fixed effects λt\lambda_{t} absorb common macroeconomic and seasonal shocks. The coefficients πℓ\pi_{\ell} and ρℓ\rho_{\ell} measure the effect of contract review on GitHub Copilot adoption and employment at horizon ℓ\ell relative to firms that have not yet reached their scheduled review. Because contract reviews are staggered over time, conventional two-way fixed-effects estimators can be biased when treatment effects vary across cohorts or over time (Miyaji, 2024b). We therefore estimate Equations (3) and (4) using the imputation estimator of Borusyak et al. (2024), which is robust to treatment effect heterogeneity. Cohorts with contract reviews after 2023 serve as our last-treated comparison group, entering the sample only prior to their review date (RiR_{i}). All regressions are unweighted and thus represent effects across firms rather than employment-weighted effects. Standard errors are clustered at the firm level.

Under parallel trends and no anticipation in employment outcomes, the reduced form coefficient ρℓ\rho_{\ell} identifies the intention-to-treat (ITT) effect of reaching a scheduled GitHub contract review on employment. Parallel trends requires that, absent a contract review, employment trajectories do not vary systematically with a firm’s scheduled review date. No anticipation requires that firms do not adjust employment ahead of an approaching contract review. The reduced form is informative even without interpreting contract review as an instrument: it captures the intention-to-treat effect of reaching a scheduled opportunity to evaluate and procure GitHub Copilot on employment outcomes.

To move from the intent-to-treat effect to the effect of adopting GitHub Copilot itself, we scale the reduced-form estimates by the first-stage adoption response using the horizon-specific Wald ratio:

θ^ℓ=ρ^ℓπ^ℓ\widehat{\theta}_{\ell}=\frac{\widehat{\rho}_{\ell}}{\widehat{\pi}_{\ell}} (5)

We construct 95% percentile confidence intervals for the Wald estimates using a firm-block bootstrap with 1,000 draws that re-estimates both legs and their ratio on the same subsample.

Interpreting θ^ℓ\widehat{\theta}_{\ell} as a causal treatment effect requires standard instrumental variables assumptions adapted to a staggered panel setting (Miyaji, 2024a; Miyaji, 2024b). Parallel trends and no anticipation must also hold for adoption.88 8 No anticipation does not rule out adoption before review; it requires that firms not time adoption in response to an approaching review. Contract review must increase adoption on average (relevance), must not delay adoption for any firm (monotonicity), and must affect employment only through GitHub Copilot adoption (exclusion). Finally, employment outcomes at horizon ℓ\ell depend on current adoption status rather than the specific duration of prior exposure (no carryover) (Miyaji, 2024a). Under these conditions, θ^ℓ\widehat{\theta}_{\ell} identifies the horizon-specific local average treatment effect on the treated (LATET) among compliers at horizon ℓ\ell (Miyaji, 2024a; Miyaji, 2024b). In our setting, compliers are firms that adopted GitHub Copilot once their scheduled review lowered the administrative hurdle, but would not yet have adopted off-cycle absent the review. For these firms, θ^ℓ\widehat{\theta}_{\ell} captures the effect of having adopted GitHub Copilot by horizon ℓ\ell relative to not yet having adopted. We evaluate the plausibility of these assumptions in Sections 4.3, 4.4, and 6.1.3.

4.3   First Stage: Contract Review and GitHub Copilot Adoption

Figure 3 plots the first stage event study from Equation (3) (for quarterly estimates, see Column 2 Appendix Table A.9). Reaching a scheduled contract review steadily increases GitHub Copilot adoption, raising the probability of adoption by 8.6 percentage points after six months and 19.3 percentage points after twelve months, both significant increases relative to the 62% end-of-sample adoption rate. At the four-quarter horizon, the first-stage FF-statistic is 30.7, well above standard weak-instrument thresholds.99 9 In our just-identified setting with firm-clustered standard errors, the squared first stage tt-statistic equals the Montiel Olea and Pflueger (2013) effective FF-statistic, for which 23.1 is the critical value for 10% worst-case bias. Whereas adjustments to existing GitHub Enterprise license counts are clustered in the two months after the contract review month, the first-stage effect on GitHub Copilot adoption builds more gradually. Updating seat counts on an existing agreement is a routine administrative change, whereas a scheduled review initiates the evaluation of GitHub Copilot as a new AI product, which requires setting up the software and rolling it out to employees.

In a standard event study, pre-period coefficients (ℓ<0\ell<0) provide a test of anticipation. In our setting, however, two distinct forces might generate the upward slope prior to a scheduled contract review in Figure 3. First, there is a mechanical composition effect from GitHub Copilot’s January 2023 launch. Before January 2023, GitHub Copilot was not available, so off-cycle adoption was not possible and adoption is identically zero. After January 2023, however, always-takers could begin adopting off-cycle prior to their scheduled review. Thus, as event time moves from ℓ=−12\ell=-12 to ℓ=−1\ell=-1, a growing share of firm-month observations fall after January 2023: at ℓ=−12\ell=-12, nearly all observations occur in 2022 when adoption is mechanically zero, whereas by ℓ=−2\ell=-2, most observations occur in 2023 when off-cycle adoption can accumulate.1010 10 This means that while the share of “always takers” in the sample may remain constant, the share able to adopt off cycle changes. This shifting sample composition may by itself create an upward slope in the pre-review leads. Second, firms might genuinely be adopting GitHub Copilot at higher rates in anticipation of their approaching contract review. Because the baseline pre-review leads mix pre-launch zeros (December 2022 and prior) with post-launch observations (January 2023 and after), the pre-period coefficients cannot distinguish anticipation directly.

To isolate and test for anticipation directly, we restrict the sample to post-January 2023 months, when off-cycle adoption was feasible for all firms. Because adoption is an absorbing state, cumulative adoption in Figure 3 accumulates all prior adoptions over time. As a result, even a constant rate of off-cycle adoption will cause the cumulative share of adopters to drift upward as the review date approaches. By contrast, the monthly adoption hazard measures the flow into adoption in a given month: among firms that have not yet adopted entering month tt, it is the fraction that adopt GitHub Copilot for the first time during month tt among those who have not yet adopted in the prior month. If firms were timing their adoption in anticipation of an approaching contract review, this monthly hazard rate would rise in the months leading up to the review. However, among firms who have not yet adopted, the pre-review monthly adoption hazard is flat at roughly 4% across the months leading up to scheduled contract review and jumps sharply in the review month itself (ℓ=0\ell=0). This pattern shows no evidence of anticipation. Estimating hazard ratios in a complementary log-log model that controls for months since GitHub Copilot’s launch shows an equally flat pre-review profile (Appendix Figure A.6).

4.4   Covariate Balance Across Contract Review Timing

Our identification strategy requires that, absent a contract review, firms scheduled for review at different dates would have followed parallel employment trajectories. While baseline covariate balance cannot verify parallel trends directly, it can help evaluate whether review timing is systematically related to pre-launch firm characteristics or employment growth.

Panel A of Figure 5 illustrates the differences by adoption status. Compared to non-adopters, eventual adopters were substantially larger, had higher baseline hiring and separation rates, employed a higher share of software engineers and a lower share of junior workers, and were more concentrated in the information technology sector. In contrast, Panel B compares firms with an early contract review to firms with a later review, split at the median contract review month of June 2023. Across all workforce composition, hiring, separation, and industry measures, the standardized differences are small and within the conventional 0.10 threshold for covariate balance (Austin, 2009).

The exception is firm size: firms with early contract reviews have log headcount that is 0.24 standard deviations higher than firms reviewed later. This pattern reflects how initial enterprise GitHub contracts were signed years prior to GitHub Copilot’s launch. Because sales commissions scale with contract value, enterprise sales teams prioritized the largest accounts early in the calendar year, and subsequent annual reviews remained anchored to those initial signing months. In our baseline specification, firm fixed effects absorb time-invariant size differences across firms, though they do not rule out differential employment trends by firm size. In Section 6.1.3, we add baseline firm-size-by-quarter fixed effects, as well as industry-by-quarter fixed effects, and show that our results are unchanged.

5   Conceptual Framework

To guide our empirical analysis, we introduce a simple accounting framework that decomposes GitHub Copilot’s effect on firm employment into three channels: the scale of software activity, the allocation of tasks across roles and seniority levels, and worker productivity.1111 11 Because our empirical design captures short run firm adjustments rather than economy-wide equilibrium responses in wages and employment, we use an accounting identity rather than an equilibrium model.

Let TiT_{i} denote the total volume of software-related tasks at firm ii. Workers are grouped into cells (r,s)(r,s) defined by role rr and seniority ss. Let mi,r​sm_{i,rs} be the share of software-related work assigned to cell (r,s)(r,s), with ∑r,smi,r​s=1\sum_{r,s}m_{i,rs}=1. Finally, ai,r​sa_{i,rs} is task-level productivity, defined as the number of tasks completed per unit of labor in that cell. Given this structure, the labor the firm requires in a particular role-by-seniority cell is:

Li,r​s=mi,r​s​Tiai,r​s.L_{i,rs}=\frac{m_{i,rs}T_{i}}{a_{i,rs}}. (6)

Taking logs and differencing with respect to a firm-level GitHub Copilot adoption (Δ\Delta) gives:

Δ​ln⁡Li,r​s=Δ​ln⁡Ti⏟scale+Δ​ln⁡mi,r​s⏟task reallocation−Δ​ln⁡ai,r​s⏟productivity.\Delta\ln L_{i,rs}=\underbrace{\Delta\ln T_{i}}_{\text{scale}}+\underbrace{\Delta\ln m_{i,rs}}_{\text{task reallocation}}-\underbrace{\Delta\ln a_{i,rs}}_{\text{productivity}}. (7)

Equation (7) highlights three potentially offsetting forces. First, by lowering software development costs, GitHub Copilot may induce the firm to undertake more projects, expanding total task volume (Δ​ln⁡Ti>0\Delta\ln T_{i}>0) and raising labor demand proportionally across all cells. Second, GitHub Copilot may alter task allocation (Δ​ln⁡mi,r​s\Delta\ln m_{i,rs}). For example, senior engineers might use GitHub Copilot to handle implementation work previously delegated to junior engineers, or developers might absorb testing tasks previously assigned to quality assurance teams. Third, GitHub Copilot changes task productivity (Δ​ln⁡ai,r​s\Delta\ln a_{i,rs}).1212 12 In principle, the effect on task-level productivity could be positive or negative. While GitHub Copilot may speed up code generation, effective productivity could fall (Δ​ln⁡ai,r​s<0\Delta\ln a_{i,rs}<0). Completing assigned tasks faster reduces the labor required for a given workload, whereas spending extra time reviewing and debugging AI-generated code lowers effective productivity and increases labor requirements.

This framework clarifies what our empirical estimates can and cannot identify. In the data, we observe employment and hiring in each cell (Li,r​sL_{i,rs}), but we do not observe the firm’s total volume of software work (TiT_{i}), how tasks are divided across cells (mi,r​sm_{i,rs}), or task-level productivity (ai,r​sa_{i,rs}). Consequently, our estimates for any single group capture the combined net effect of all three channels. However, comparing employment responses across cells within the same firm, such as junior versus experienced engineers in the same role, differences out the firm-wide scale effect (Δ​ln⁡Ti\Delta\ln T_{i}), which is common to all cells in firm ii. Any divergence across groups within a firm must therefore reflect differential changes in task allocation (Δ​ln⁡mi,r​s\Delta\ln m_{i,rs}) or task-level productivity (Δ​ln⁡ai,r​s\Delta\ln a_{i,rs}). Finally, because hiring decisions are forward-looking, our short-run estimates cannot separate responses to realized productivity gains from adjustments driven by managers’ beliefs and expectations about AI capabilities. As firms learn about the tool’s actual performance and as project scale and task allocation adjust at different speeds, these net employment effects may evolve over longer horizons.

6   Results

6.1   Overall Effects on the Technical Workforce

6.1.1   Hiring, Separations, and Headcount

We first examine how a scheduled contract review affects overall technical employment flows and stocks. Figure 6 plots the monthly reduced form coefficient of technical hiring and separations. Panel A shows that the reduced form hiring coefficients turn negative approximately five months after a scheduled contract review. By month twelve, technical hiring is 7.6% (−0.079-0.079 log points) lower relative to firms that have not yet reached their scheduled review (Table , Column 1). Panel B shows no corresponding increase in separations, which include both voluntary and involuntary worker exits: at month twelve, the point estimate is a statistically insignificant 2.9% (0.0290.029 log points; Column 3). The 95% confidence interval rules out separation increases larger than roughly 12%. See Appendix Table A.10 for the full monthly coefficients. Together, these results show that firms adjust their technical workforce after a contract review by slowing new hiring rather than increasing separations.

Columns (2) and (4) of Table show no evidence of a corresponding change on the extensive margin of either hiring or separations (Appendix Figure A.7 plots the full extensive margin event studies). On average, firms continue to hire technical workers each month, but in smaller numbers.

We find no statistically detectable change in total technical headcount twelve months after a contract review, with a point estimate of −0.016-0.016 log points, or a 1.6% decline (Column 5 of Table ). The point estimate on headcount is exactly what would be implied by the slowdown in hiring. The average firm in our sample employs 823 technical workers and hires 17.7 technical workers per month. As an illustrative calculation, applying the estimated 7.6% hiring decline to this mean, while holding the probability of hiring and separations fixed, implies approximately 1.35 fewer hires per month, or 16 fewer hires over a year. This cumulative shortfall would reduce technical headcount by approximately 2% after one year, close to the estimated 1.6% decline. If sustained, the same hiring shortfall would produce a headcount gap of roughly 3.5% after about two years, approximately the magnitude needed for statistical significance at the 5% level given the current standard error, although both the effect and its precision may change at longer horizons. These results confirm that because monthly hiring flows represent a minor fraction of overall headcount, even sizable declines in hiring translate into modest cumulative effects on total workforce size over a one-year horizon.

Scaling these reduced form estimates by the first stage yields the implied effect of GitHub Copilot adoption on hiring flows among compliers. The month-twelve Wald estimate indicates that having adopted GitHub Copilot by month twelve reduces monthly technical hiring by approximately 34% among compliers. In the quarterly specification, which we use for our disaggregated analyses below, the fourth-quarter Wald estimate is −0.340-0.340 log points, or a 29% decline in quarterly technical hiring, with a 95% firm-block bootstrap confidence interval of [−0.948, 0.088][-0.948,\,0.088] log points (Appendix Table A.9 reports the full quarterly path). While the horizon-specific Wald ratios are similar in magnitude across quarters, their bootstrap intervals are wide, so the estimates cannot distinguish an immediate, constant effect from one that builds with exposure. Nor can our design separate the two, since identifying the duration of exposure would need additional instruments beyond the timing of contract review. Overall, although the Wald ratios are less precisely estimated than the reduced form because they compound sampling variation from both stages, both sets of estimates point to gradual workforce adjustment through lower hiring rather than worker quits or layoffs.

6.1.2   Recruiting Activity, Vacancy Duration, and Incidence

Realized hiring reflects both how many positions firms seek to fill and how quickly they fill open vacancies. A decline in hiring could therefore reflect either lower labor demand or a slower matching process, for instance if AI adoption induced firms to search for scarcer candidates with AI-specific skills. To distinguish between these explanations, Appendix Table A.11 reports the reduced form effects of a scheduled contract review on three quarterly measures of technical recruiting activity: job postings, duration postings remain open, and any posting activity. Four quarters after a scheduled contract review, the intensive margin of open technical postings falls by 14% (−0.148-0.148 log points). In contrast, contract review has no statistically detectable effect on the probability of having any open technical posting or the time a posting is open, although there are some pre-trends in posting duration. The slowdown in technical hiring seems to be driven by firms opening fewer positions rather than taking longer to fill existing vacancies.

Taken together, the employment flow and job posting results show that GitHub Copilot adoption initially slows technical workforce growth by reducing new hiring rather than displacing incumbent workers. Although the direct incidence of this adjustment falls on prospective hires, incumbent workers may still be affected indirectly. As hiring slows across adopting firms, fewer outside job openings can narrow incumbents’ outside options, reducing job-to-job mobility and weakening wage bargaining within the firm (Caldwell and Danieli, 2024; Jäger et al., 2024). Concentrating adjustment on the hiring margin could be consistent with models of labor demand with quasi-fixed labor costs or AI coding assistance devaluing the skills of novices (Oi, 1962; Abowd et al., 1999).

6.1.3   Placebo and Robustness Checks

We evaluate three alternative explanations to verify that the decline in technical hiring reflects GitHub Copilot adoption rather than recurring corporate budgeting cycles, contemporaneous firm-wide hiring freezes or general AI procurement, or differential trends by firm size and sector. First, scheduled contract reviews could in principle coincide with annual corporate budgeting or fiscal planning dates when firms routinely reset hiring targets. To test this directly, we conduct a pre-launch placebo check by assigning each firm its scheduled contract review date prior to GitHub Copilot’s 2023 launch. Although this restricts the post-review window to two quarters before GitHub Copilot’s launch, a recurring budget-driven contraction decided at the contract review should begin to register in realized hiring within that timeframe. Instead, we find no effects on overall technical hiring, separations, or junior and experienced software engineering hiring (Appendix Table A.17). Moreover, even after GitHub Copilot’s release, the technical hiring decline does not appear as an immediate adjustment at the review date, as an annual budget reset would imply, but instead emerges gradually in the third and fourth quarters after review, tracking the rollout of GitHub Copilot licenses.

Second, even if pre-launch reviews did not affect employment, a firm’s 2023 review might coincide with a broader post-2022 white-collar hiring freeze, an IT-wide budget cut, or the simultaneous procurement of general office AI tools (although GitHub Copilot was the only AI product sold by GitHub’s dedicated sales force). To test for firm-wide shocks, we examine hiring for accountants, the most common non-technical professional occupation in our data (employed by 98% of sample firms, with a pre-launch median of 34 per firm) and one exposed to both general AI tools and broader white-collar hiring slowdowns. Appendix Figure A.12 shows no decline in either log accountant hires or the probability of hiring an accountant following contract review. Four quarters after review, the reduced-form estimate for log accountant hiring is a statistically insignificant 0.0350.035 log points. Furthermore, as we show in Section 6.2, the slowdown is not uniform even within the technical workforce: hiring is unchanged in less code-intensive technical roles and among experienced engineers, weighing against a broad technical or IT-department hiring freeze.

Third, because firms with earlier contract-review dates have larger pre-launch workforces, our estimates could be confounded if larger and smaller firms, or different sectors, followed distinct post-launch hiring trajectories. In Appendix Table A.18, we re-estimate our specifications adding interactions between calendar-quarter fixed effects and pre-launch firm-size terciles, indicators for the information and professional-services sectors, or both. Across all specifications, the four-quarter reduced-form estimates for total technical hiring and separations change by at most 0.0080.008 log points (Columns 1 and 2), confirming that differential trends by firm size or sector do not drive our findings.

6.2   Hiring Composition by Code Intensity and Seniority

The preceding results show that GitHub Copilot adoption reduces overall technical hiring. We next examine whether this decline is spread evenly across the technical workforce or concentrated among particular roles and seniority levels, changing the composition of new hires.

6.2.1   Measuring the Coding Content of Technical Work

We define a position’s code intensity as the share of its described responsibilities devoted to activities within GitHub Copilot’s core domain during our study period: writing, completing, testing, documenting, explaining, and debugging code. To measure code intensity across roles and seniority levels, we use the text of LinkedIn position descriptions for technical jobs at sample firms with start dates between 2018 and 2022, prior to GitHub Copilot’s launch.1313 13 Because LinkedIn users can edit position descriptions retrospectively, some text may have been written or revised after GitHub Copilot’s launch; our sample restriction applies to the position’s start date. Unlike occupation-level task measures that assign a single average to a broad occupational code, position descriptions capture how responsibilities vary both across granular technical roles and across seniority levels within a role. Appendix Figure A.8 illustrates this variation using examples from outside our sample: a software engineer describes building a job-scheduling platform and implementing APIs (Panel A), whereas a test automation engineer combines programming in Python and LabVIEW with physical design and testing of liquid-nitrogen heat exchangers (Panel B). Similarly, within infrastructure engineering, a technical lead describes setting team strategy and recruiting, while a technical lead manager combines engineering management with building machine learning infrastructure (Panels C and D).

We score each description on this dimension using Claude Sonnet 4.6 (see Appendix Section B.10 for the prompt and implementation details). The model observes only the free-text description, without the job title, occupation, seniority, location, firm, or start date. For our baseline cross-role analysis, we average the description-level scores within each of the eight technical roles. Code intensity is thus an ex ante measure of task overlap with GitHub Copilot’s capabilities rather than a measure of actual time spent coding or realized GitHub Copilot usage.

Figure 7 reports average code intensity by technical role. Roles whose primary output is software code receive the highest scores, led by software engineering (47%), application development (36%), data engineering (33%), and quality assurance engineering (22%). We refer to these four roles above the median as code-intensive roles. Coding is less central in infrastructure engineering (19%), cybersecurity engineering (15%), systems engineering (7%), and design engineering (5%), which, in our sample, primarily captures hardware, silicon, and product design roles where programming supports broader operational, security, or physical engineering responsibilities.

6.2.2   Hiring Responses by Role and Seniority

A large empirical literature measures AI exposure at the occupation level by scoring the share of an occupation’s tasks that overlap with AI capabilities (Eloundou et al., 2024; Felten et al., 2023). If occupation-level task overlap directly governs how AI shifts labor demand, hiring responses should vary systematically with a role’s pre-launch code intensity. However, pooling all hires within a role may obscure heterogeneity across seniority levels, either because firms reduce junior hiring uniformly across technical roles as in cyclical downturns (Forsythe, 2022), or because GitHub Copilot substitutes more readily for the coding tasks performed by junior workers than for those bundled into experienced roles. To evaluate how role code intensity and worker seniority shape hiring, we construct a firm-by-role-by-seniority-by-quarter panel and estimate:

Yi​r​s​t=αi​r​s+λr​s​t+∑ℓ[ρℓ+γℓJuniors+θℓxr+βℓ(Juniors×xr)]𝟏{t−Ri=ℓ}+ui​r​s​tY_{irst}=\alpha_{irs}+\lambda_{rst}+\sum_{\ell}\left[\rho_{\ell}+\gamma_{\ell}\mathrm{Junior}_{s}+\theta_{\ell}x_{r}+\beta_{\ell}\left(\mathrm{Junior}_{s}\times x_{r}\right)\right]\mathbf{1}\{t-R_{i}=\ell\}+u_{irst} (8)

where Yi​r​s​tY_{irst} is log quarterly hires for firm ii, role rr, seniority group ss, and quarter tt in cells with positive hiring. There are two seniority groups: Juniors\mathrm{Junior}_{s} equals one for junior positions (Revelio seniority levels 1 and 2, covering interns, trainees, and early-career workers) and zero for experienced positions (levels 3 and above). The specification includes firm-by-role-by-seniority fixed effects αi​r​s\alpha_{irs} and role-by-seniority-by-quarter fixed effects λr​s​t\lambda_{rst}.

Table reports the quarter-four estimates across these specifications. Column (1) begins with a role-level benchmark that pools across seniority on a firm-by-role-by-quarter panel with firm-by-role and role-by-quarter fixed effects. Four quarters after contract review, a one-standard-deviation increase in role code intensity is associated with a statistically insignificant −0.023-0.023 log-point difference in hiring (SE=0.022\text{SE}=0.022). If ex ante task overlap with GitHub Copilot’s capabilities were a sufficient summary of labor substitutability, hiring declines should be steepest in the most coding-intensive roles. Instead, role-level code intensity alone does not reliably predict where hiring falls. Column (2) tests for a uniform shift away from junior hiring across all technical roles and similarly finds a small, statistically insignificant junior-experienced differential (−0.013-0.013 log points, SE=0.040\text{SE}=0.040). Neither occupation-level code intensity nor worker seniority alone predicts where hiring falls.

A sharper pattern emerges in Column (3), which interacts role code intensity with seniority. Among experienced positions, the estimated code-intensity gradient θ4\theta_{4} is a statistically insignificant 0.0150.015 log points. Among junior positions, however, the coding-intensity slope is 0.0860.086 log points more negative than the experienced slope (β4=−0.086\beta_{4}=-0.086). Combining these terms, a one-standard-deviation increase in role code intensity is associated with a 0.0710.071 log-point larger decline in junior hiring. Column (4) replaces the continuous score xrx_{r} with an indicator for the four code-intensive roles above the median: the junior-experienced hiring differential is 0.2270.227 log points more negative in code-intensive roles than in less code-intensive roles, and the implied high-minus-low contrast in junior hiring is −0.180-0.180 log points. Because the two role groups sit 1.6 standard deviations apart on the score, the Column (3) slope implies a high-low contrast of about 0.140.14 log points, which is very close to the continuous estimate.

Figure 8 plots the separate four-quarter reduced-form hiring estimates for each of the 16 role-by-seniority cells, ordered by role code intensity. While the individual cell estimates are noisier than the pooled regression, they show a consistent pattern across the role distribution rather than a single outlier occupation. In Panel A, the point estimates for junior hiring are negative in all four code-intensive roles and positive in all four less code-intensive roles, whereas Panel B shows no comparable ordering across roles for experienced hiring.

This divergence is robust across alternative measures and within-firm specifications. Although junior positions in code-intensive roles involve somewhat more coding than experienced positions in the same role (Appendix Figure A.9), replacing the role-level score xrx_{r} with cell-specific pre-launch coding-intensity scores xr​sx_{rs} leaves the estimates nearly unchanged: the junior gradient is −0.062-0.062 log points, the experienced gradient is 0.0200.020 log points, and their difference is −0.082-0.082 log points (Columns 1 and 2 of Appendix Table A.12).

To isolate how an individual firm adjusts the seniority mix within a role, we also re-estimate the model using the within-firm log junior-to-experienced hiring ratio, log⁡(Hi​r​tJ/Hi​r​tE)\log(H_{irt}^{J}/H_{irt}^{E}), among firms that hire both groups in role rr and quarter tt, which differences out any firm-by-role-by-quarter shock that scales hiring proportionally across seniority levels. Four quarters after contract review, a one-standard-deviation increase in role code intensity reduces a firm’s junior-to-experienced hiring ratio by 7.7% (−0.080-0.080 log points, p<0.05p<0.05; Column 3 of Appendix Table A.12), and an indicator for the four code-intensive roles reduces the ratio by 15.5% (−0.169-0.169 log points, p<0.05p<0.05; Column 4 and Appendix Figure A.10).

Across role groups, contract review does not affect the probability of positive quarterly hiring or of hiring both junior and experienced workers in the same quarter, confirming that our intensive-margin and ratio estimates are not driven by extensive-margin selection (Appendix Table A.13). Finally, as in Section 6.1.3, these role-by-seniority estimates show no pre-launch placebo effects and are unchanged when adding firm-size-by-quarter and industry-by-quarter fixed effects (Appendix Tables A.17 and A.18).

6.2.3   Implied Magnitudes and Compositional Shifts

Because the hiring contraction is concentrated among junior positions in code-intensive roles, GitHub Copilot adoption reshapes both the entry paths of junior workers and the seniority structure of technical teams (Figure 9). At baseline, 72% of all junior technical hires enter through code-intensive roles; with GitHub Copilot adoption, that share falls to 52%, leaving entry-level hiring nearly evenly split between more and less code-intensive roles while the role mix of experienced hiring is largely unchanged (69% to 74% code-intensive; Panel A). Viewed within role groups, the junior share of code-intensive hiring drops from 57% to 45%, whereas the junior share in less code-intensive roles rises from 54% to 68% (Panel B). In level terms (Panel C), junior hiring in code-intensive roles drops by about 7 spells per firm-quarter, while experienced hiring in these roles is fairly flat. Comparing the two ends of the coding-intensity distribution directly illustrates this divergence (Appendix Table A.14; see Appendix Figure A.11 for the monthly reduced form event studies). GitHub Copilot adoption reduces quarterly junior software engineering hiring by approximately 40% (−0.513-0.513 log points), with no detectable decline among experienced software engineers (−0.160-0.160 log points) or systems and infrastructure engineers (0.2120.212 log points).

Through the lens of our conceptual framework, a common change in the scale of software production cannot explain why junior and experienced hiring diverge within the same role. Instead, this divergence reflects differences across seniority levels in task-level productivity gains, job bundling, or task allocation. First, GitHub Copilot may generate larger direct labor-saving productivity gains on the coding tasks typically assigned to junior workers. Second, junior and experienced positions differ in how coding is bundled with other responsibilities, which explains why the seniority gap persists even when coding intensity is measured at the role-by-seniority cell level (Garicano et al., 2026). Whereas junior positions in code-intensive roles center on discrete implementation tasks that can be specified, delegated, and evaluated independently at relatively low cost, experienced positions bundle code production with system architecture, domain judgment, and cross-team accountability. Because coding is more separable from the rest of the job in junior positions, GitHub Copilot may substitute more readily for junior hiring even if it improves productivity in both groups.

At the same time, the flat code-intensity gradient for experienced hiring does not imply that GitHub Copilot leaves experienced work unchanged or simply complements experienced labor. Even as GitHub Copilot saves experienced engineers time on their existing coding tasks, firms may expand the scope of work assigned to them, or change their time allocation. Experienced engineers may use GitHub Copilot to complete implementation work previously delegated to junior teammates, or spend more time reviewing, debugging, and integrating AI-generated code alongside their core architectural and coordination duties. These offsetting forces, labor savings on existing coding tasks alongside task reallocation from junior positions and new verification demands, could leave net experienced hiring approximately flat across the code-intensity distribution even as GitHub Copilot reshapes their day-to-day work.

6.3   Experience, Credentials, and Internal Hiring among Software Engineers

Although firms maintain their volume of experienced software engineering hires after adopting GitHub Copilot, stable hiring volume could mask changes in the types of engineers firms recruit. Within software engineering, the largest and most code-intensive occupation in our sample, we next examine whether firms adjust the educational credentials, prior experience, and internal sourcing of the workers they hire. At baseline, experienced software engineers average 8.7 years since earning their bachelor’s degree, compared with 4.8 years among junior engineers, and are significantly more likely to hold an academic master’s or doctoral degree (Appendix Table A.15).

In principle, AI coding tools could either substitute for or complement accumulated general and firm-specific human capital. If GitHub Copilot makes programming knowledge and codebase conventions readily accessible on the job, firms may relax degree, experience, or internal-tenure requirements when filling positions. Conversely, if deeper technical training, industry experience, or familiarity with the firm’s architecture makes engineers more effective at directing AI tools, evaluating generated code, and coordinating system design, firms could raise the bar on these qualifications among new hires.

Panel A of Table 1 tests these predictions by estimating the reduced form effect of contract review, pooling the third and fourth quarters after review, on the education and experience of software engineering hires. Among junior software engineering positions (Column 1), where total hiring falls sharply, we find no statistically detectable change in the educational credentials or prior experience of the workers who are hired. Among experienced positions (Column 2), by contrast, stable total hiring masks a shift toward candidates with greater general human capital. The share of experienced hires holding a graduate degree rises by 4.7 percentage points, and the share who are at least five years past their bachelor’s degree rises by a similar magnitude. On average, newly hired experienced software engineers have 1.28 additional years of potential experience since completing their bachelor’s degree. Rather than lowering qualification thresholds, firms raise the bar for experienced software engineering roles.

Panel B examines whether firms also shift toward internal candidates who possess firm-specific human capital or whose capabilities are better known to the firm (Becker, 1962; Li et al., 2026). We define a position fill as internal if the worker held a position at the same firm in the prior year, such as an internship or prior full time role, and as external otherwise. Among experienced software engineering positions, external hires fall by approximately 13%, whereas internal fills do not show statistically significant change. Among junior positions, both internal and external fills decline by similar proportions, with no statistically distinguishable shift toward internal sourcing.

Together, Panels A and B reveal an asymmetry in how firms adjust their software engineering workforce across the seniority distribution. Firms reduce the quantity of junior software engineering hires without changing their observable qualifications, while maintaining the volume of experienced hires and upgrading their education, prior experience, and internal tenure. Although AI coding assistants may deliver large task-level productivity gains to novices in experimental settings, in practice they may complement accumulated general and firm-specific human capital.

6.4   Geographic Composition of Technical Hiring

Beyond shifting the roles, seniority, and credentials of new hires, AI coding assistants could also reshape where firms locate technical work. Firms in our sample employ technical workers both domestically and offshore, with India the most common offshore location. During 2021–2022, approximately 58% of firms employed at least one technical worker in India, while 83% employed at least one worker there in any occupation. This concentration reflects India’s emergence as a leading global hub for offshore software development. Beginning in the early 2000s, India developed a large export-oriented software services industry, supported by a substantial pool of English-speaking engineers, strong technical universities, and labor costs well below those in the United States and Europe (Arora and Gambardella, 2005; Parthasarathy, 2013).

In principle, AI coding assistants could disproportionately benefit offshore workers through several channels. First, LLMs can facilitate communication across language barriers, reducing coordination costs associated with geographically distributed engineering teams (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025b). Second, coding assistants can help workers interpret technical specifications, navigate unfamiliar codebases, and understand internal systems. These capabilities may be particularly valuable for offshore engineers, who often have less access to the informal knowledge and institutional context available to colleagues at a firm’s headquarters. Third, given substantial wage differentials between domestic and offshore engineers, AI tools that reduce these productivity and coordination disadvantages could make offshore labor an even more attractive substitute for domestic labor.

On the other hand, tasks that can be performed offshore may be more easily codified and therefore more susceptible to automation. Moreover, firms may be more willing to reduce hiring outside their headquarters country, where reputational concerns, social pressures, and information frictions may impose fewer constraints on employment adjustments (Landier et al., 2009; Bassanini et al., 2017).

To examine this margin, Appendix Table A.16 estimates the effects of contract review on technical hiring in firms’ headquarters countries (“domestic”) and India, restricting the sample to the 4,509 firms with a presence in India during the pre-period. The reduced-form estimates are imprecise, partly reflecting the smaller sample and sparser hiring abroad, and do not reveal statistically significant differences in hiring responses across locations. Four quarters after contract review, the point estimate for India-based technical hiring is −0.060-0.060 log points (SE=0.189\text{SE}=0.189), compared with −0.029-0.029 log points for domestic technical hiring. Although the estimates are too imprecise to detect differences across locations reliably, they provide no evidence of a shift toward offshore technical hiring following GitHub Copilot adoption. If anything, the point estimates suggest a larger slowdown in India.

6.5   Contribution of GitHub Copilot to the Overall Decline in Technical Hiring

Finally, we benchmark our treatment effect estimates against the broader post-2022 contraction in technical recruiting. Between 2022 and 2024, our last full calendar year in the data, mean quarterly technical hiring across sample firms fell by 29%, or 16.1 hires per firm-quarter (from 55.3 to 39.2). To evaluate how much of this aggregate slowdown can be attributed to GitHub Copilot adoption, we use our treatment effect estimates to impute counterfactual post-period hiring. Let Hi​0H_{i0} and Hi​1H_{i1} denote mean quarterly technical hires at firm ii in 2022 and 2024, and let Hi​1​(0)H_{i1}(0) denote the hires firm ii would have made in 2024 had it not adopted GitHub Copilot. We decompose the observed decline in mean quarterly hiring per firm, Δ\Delta, into a component attributable to GitHub Copilot adoption and a residual component capturing other factors:

Δ=1N​∑i(Hi​0−Hi​1)=1N​∑i(Hi​1​(0)−Hi​1)⏟ΔGitHub Copilot+1N​∑i(Hi​0−Hi​1​(0))⏟ΔOther.\Delta=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\big(H_{i0}-H_{i1}\big)=\underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\big(H_{i1}(0)-H_{i1}\big)}_{\Delta_{\text{GitHub Copilot}}}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\big(H_{i0}-H_{i1}(0)\big)}_{\Delta_{\text{Other}}}. (9)

For non-adopters, Hi​1​(0)=Hi​1H_{i1}(0)=H_{i1}, so only adopters contribute to ΔGitHub Copilot\Delta_{\text{GitHub Copilot}}. For a firm with an estimated log hiring effect βi​1\beta_{i1}, counterfactual hiring without adoption is Hi​1​(0)=Hi​1​e−βi​1H_{i1}(0)=H_{i1}e^{-\beta_{i1}}, and its forgone hiring is Hi​1​(e−βi​1−1)H_{i1}(e^{-\beta_{i1}}-1). We evaluate forgone hiring across the event quarters following each firm’s 2023 contract review (ℓ=0,…,4\ell=0,\dots,4) and average across quarters and firms to obtain Δ^GitHub Copilot\hat{\Delta}_{\text{GitHub Copilot}}. See Appendix Section F for additional details and caveats.

Figure 10 reports ΔGitHub Copilot\Delta_{\text{GitHub Copilot}} under three progressively stronger assumptions about which firms the estimated effects apply to:

  1. 1.

    Reduced form counterfactual. Applying the reduced-form coefficient ρ^\hat{\rho} to all firms captures the intent-to-treat effect of reaching a scheduled contract review. This generates 1.7 forgone hires per firm-quarter or 10% of the overall aggregate decline.

  2. 2.

    Wald, compliers counterfactual. Applying the Wald estimate θ^\hat{\theta} to adopting firms, scaled by the complier share of adopters, attributes 3 forgone hires per firm-quarter, or 19% of the overall decline, to GitHub Copilot. Because adopting firms are larger and hire more workers at baseline than non-adopters, these estimates are larger than the reduced form benchmark.

  3. 3.

    Wald, all adopters counterfactual. This makes the stronger assumption that all adopters experience the same proportional hiring decline and path as compliers. This produces an estimated reduction to 8.1 hires per firm-quarter, or 51% of the overall decline.

A simple back-of-the-envelope calculation grounds this third benchmark: because our fourth-quarter treatment effect is similar in magnitude to the overall 2022 to 2024 hiring decline (29%) and roughly half of the sample had adopted GitHub Copilot by 2024, applying the complier effect to all adopters accounts for about half of the aggregate slowdown, with half driven by other macroeconomic factors.

We emphasize that these calculations are illustrative benchmarks rather than exact counterfactuals for four reasons. First, treatment effects are estimated in event time over the year following each firm’s 2023 contract review (spanning 2023Q1 through 2024Q4 across cohorts), whereas the aggregate decline Δ\Delta is measured between calendar years 2022 and 2024. The decomposition therefore treats the average effect over the first year post-review as the average effect in the 2024 post-period. Second, ρ^ℓ\widehat{\rho}_{\ell} and θ^ℓ\widehat{\theta}_{\ell} are estimated in logs on unweighted firm-quarters with positive hiring, so applying them to firm hiring levels assumes treatment effects are homogeneous across firms. Third, the all-adopters benchmark (Appendix Equation (12)) does not have a clean upper bound. Because always-takers adopt earlier on average than compliers, they may have initially deployed earlier, less capable versions of the tool, or benefit more from the scale effects of AI adoption, leading to smaller hiring reductions. On the other hand, they could have larger hiring slowdowns. Fourth, the calculation is partial equilibrium: it treats the hiring of non-adopting firms as invariant to adoption elsewhere, whereas in equilibrium some candidates not hired by adopting firms may be absorbed by other employers in the sample. Finally, our design cannot separate which specific factors drove the remaining half to four-fifths of the hiring slowdown, such as monetary tightening, the correction of pandemic-era overhiring, changes in the tax treatment of software research and development, or AI adoption operating through other channels.

7   Conclusion

As AI systems become more capable, a central question is how firms adjust their workforces. Which roles will experience increases, decreases, or no change in demand? Will firms adjust on the hiring margin, by reallocating or separating from incumbent workers, or all three? We study these margins among large, technology-intensive multinational firms adopting GitHub Copilot, an early enterprise AI coding assistant, exploiting variation in the timing of pre-existing enterprise software contract reviews to identify causal effects. We find that the initial labor market adjustment occurs on the hiring margin rather than through separations. Rather than reducing recruitment uniformly, adopting firms cut entry-level hiring in code-intensive roles while maintaining the volume of experienced hires and raising the bar on their education, prior experience, and firm-specific tenure. The early impact of AI coding assistance thus appears less as broad job displacement and more as a narrowing of entry-level pipelines alongside greater demand for accumulated human capital. Thus, even when generative AI provides the largest task-level productivity boost to novices, those individual gains need not translate into greater labor demand.

Our findings also point to several open questions about how the labor market effects of AI will evolve across firms and over time. First, our estimates characterize large, established multinationals operating complex software systems. Smaller or younger firms facing fewer coordination constraints may reorganize production more rapidly, or respond to lower software development costs by expanding output and technical hiring more elastically. Second, our sample period captures the first wave of AI coding assistants, which operated primarily by autocompleting code within a developer’s workflow. Newer agentic systems capable of executing multi-step engineering tasks autonomously could deepen substitution or extend it further up the seniority distribution. Conversely, if early corporate adjustments partly reflected expectations that outpaced realized productivity gains, or if shrinking the junior cohort eventually creates bottlenecks in the supply of senior talent, firms’ hiring strategies may rebalance over a longer horizon.

Finally, our firm-level estimates do not capture wage adjustments or aggregate employment. Slower hiring and shifts in skill demand can alter compensation and the division of surplus between firms and workers even when total headcount is stable. Moreover, a contraction in a specific entry channel at large adopting firms need not translate one-for-one into lower aggregate technical employment (Raymond, 2023; Acemoglu et al., 2020). Workers who would otherwise have joined these firms as junior software engineers may instead enter adjacent roles such as systems or infrastructure engineering, or take software engineering positions at smaller or later-adopting firms. On the other hand, firms who adopt AI may steal market share from other firms. Determining how these firm-level shifts in hiring and career ladders reshape market-wide employment, wages, and long-run labor demand remains a central question for future research.

Appendix Materials – For Online Publication

Appendix A Background on GitHub and AI Coding Tools

A.1   GitHub

Pull-based software development originated in the open-source community. In 2005, Linus Torvalds released Git, a distributed version control system that allowed developers to maintain independent copies of a codebase and propose changes for integration. Three years later, Tom Preston-Werner, Chris Wanstrath, and P.J. Hyett launched GitHub as a web-based collaboration layer built on top of Git, introducing a structured pull-request workflow through which developers submit, review, and merge proposed code changes (Appendix Figure A.1). The platform grew from 100,000 users in 2009 to more than 31 million by 2018.

In its early years, GitHub served primarily as an open-source collaboration platform offering free hosting for public repositories. Commercial adoption grew out of bottom-up developer demand: as software engineers increasingly used personal GitHub accounts for workplace projects in place of legacy internal tools, corporate customers requested an enterprise version with centralized administration and security controls, prompting the launch of GitHub Enterprise in 2011. Over the following decade, the pull-request workflow became the standard model for commercial software development at large organizations. Microsoft acquired GitHub in 2018, but GitHub continued to operate as an independent business unit with its own enterprise sales force and contracting systems (Nagle et al., 2023).

A.2   AI Coding Tools

Automated code assistance predates large language models. Rule-based tools such as Microsoft’s IntelliSense, introduced in Visual Studio in 1997, provided syntax-aware identifier completion and error flagging. By 2006, code-completion tools were widely used by Java developers, although early empirical studies found that they primarily reduced documentation lookup rather than substantially accelerating code production (Murphy et al., 2006; Jiang and Coblenz, 2024). Later tools such as Tabnine introduced statistical and early deep-learning models to offer short line-by-line completions.

Large language models marked a step change in code generation capabilities. Because LLMs predict subsequent tokens conditional on surrounding context, programming languages are particularly well suited to their architecture: code follows strict syntactic and semantic rules, vast corpora of paired source code and natural-language documentation are publicly available for training, and compilers and test suites provide objective verification signals. These features supported rapid capability gains. On SWE-bench, an evaluation benchmark introduced in 2023 that tasks models with resolving real GitHub issues across 12 Python repositories, frontier model resolution rates rose from under 5% at launch to nearly 80% by early 2026 (Jimenez et al., 2024; Maslej et al., 2025).

GitHub Copilot first launched as a technical preview in June 2021 (Friedman, 2021). GitHub Copilot for Individuals became generally available in June 2022, followed by GitHub Copilot for Business for enterprise customers in early 2023. Developer uptake was rapid: in a 2023 industry survey, 56% of professional developers reported using GitHub Copilot, more than four times the share of the next most common AI coding tool (Stack Overflow, 2023). The initial version of GitHub Copilot was powered by OpenAI Codex, a model trained on billions of lines of public source code. Subsequent releases expanded the product beyond in-line autocomplete to include an interactive chat interface (Appendix Figure A.2), allowed users to select among multiple frontier models (McKenna and Perz, 2026), and enabled enterprise customers to index private repositories to ground responses in their internal codebase.

A growing body of research examines the effects of GitHub Copilot at the individual developer level; Ani et al. (2024) provide an early review. Controlled experiments and field studies evaluate its effects on task-level developer speed and output (Cui et al., 2026), the security and quality of generated code (Fu et al., 2025), and computer science education (Shah et al., 2025).

Appendix B Data Construction, Measurement, and Validation

B.1   Revelio Occupational and Seniority Measures

Workers on LinkedIn often describe similar jobs using different titles, while identical titles can correspond to different occupations across firms and industries. Revelio standardizes free-text job titles using a hierarchical clustering algorithm that incorporates job titles, text from workers’ and employers’ job descriptions, workers’ skills, coworkers, and prior experience (Revelio Labs, 2026a). For example, titles such as “Software Developer,” “Backend Engineer,” and “Full Stack Developer” are grouped into a common “Software Engineering” category. We use Revelio’s 150-cluster job taxonomy, the most granular classification recommended for firm-by-year analysis (Revelio Labs, 2026b).

We also use Revelio’s measure of worker seniority. Because titles convey different levels of seniority across firms and occupations, Revelio constructs a seniority score using an ensemble model that combines an individual’s title, company, and industry with the duration and seniority of previous employment and age (Revelio Labs, 2026b). The resulting measure ranges from entry-level to senior executive positions.1414 14 The seniority categories range from entry level (e.g., account intern, paralegal, software engineer trainee), junior (e.g., Junior Software QA Engineer, Legal Adviser), associate (e.g., attorney, senior tax accountant), manager, director, executive, and senior executive (e.g., CEO, CFO, COO) (Revelio Labs, 2026b).

From the underlying individual position spells, we construct a monthly panel of employment stocks, new hires, and separations at the firm level, as well as disaggregated panels at the firm-by-role and firm-by-role-by-seniority levels.

B.2   Revelio Coverage and Measurement

Online professional profiles over-represent white-collar and technical occupations, younger cohorts, and larger, more established firms. Coverage is particularly comprehensive in information technology and among professional, scientific, and technical workers in North America and Europe (Baird et al., 2026). These features make Revelio well suited to tracking the technical workforces of large GitHub customers. Because coverage is thinner in other regions and has grown over time with platform adoption, we restrict our sample to firms headquartered in the Americas and Europe.

In addition to raw spell counts, Revelio adjusts their data to correct for two sources of measurement error (Revelio Labs, 2026b). First, a cross-sectional sampling weight adjusts for differences in profile representation across occupations, industries, and countries. Second, a time-series adjustment accounts for reporting lags between when an employment transition occurs and when a worker updates their online profile. Both adjustments are calibrated against firm-level headcount benchmarks from regulatory filings. Throughout our analysis, we use these adjusted employment and flow series.

B.3   GitHub–Revelio Firm Matching Procedure

We link GitHub administrative records to Revelio Labs using firm name, country, industry, and size indicators. As a first step, we apply Revelio’s internal name-matching algorithm, which strips common legal suffixes (such as “LLC,” “Inc.,” and “GmbH”) and administrative tags (such as “Parent”) before performing an exact string match against standardized company names in Revelio’s database. The algorithm excludes company profile pages with zero recorded employees and, when a match corresponds to a corporate subsidiary, aggregates employment to the ultimate parent firm.

This initial string-matching step yields a high-confidence match for approximately 64% of GitHub accounts. The remaining accounts are not matched automatically because their recorded names are generic, abbreviated, or formatted differently across the two databases. Discrepancies typically arise when a firm operates under a distinct brand or division name on professional networking platforms (e.g., “ABC Inc.” versus “ABC Science”), when non-English characters or transliterations differ across systems, or when the GitHub license is held by a subsidiary whose legal name does not appear as a standalone entity in Revelio. To resolve these cases, we combine an AI-assisted matching pipeline with human verification, using firm country, industry, and employee size to identify and validate the corresponding company profile page, as detailed in the next subsection.

B.4   LinkedIn Search Algorithm

  1. 1.

    Search. Use Google’s site-specific search to search LinkedIn for the firm’s Salesforce firm name and country: site:linkedin.com/company ‘‘COMPANY_NAME’’ COUNTRY. If results are poor, search using less restrictive queries, including dropping exact search, removing company suffixes, reordering words, and using name stubs instead of full names.

  2. 2.

    Filter. Among the results, identify the company page whose name closely matches the full Salesforce account name and whose LinkedIn-reported location matches the firm’s account country. Additional suggestive criteria include whether the company page is “claimed” by an owner (and therefore not automatically generated) and larger follower and employee counts.

  3. 3.

    Record. Record the page’s LinkedIn slug from the URL (e.g., linkedin.com/company/
    activision; Figure A.3), and note possible issues with the match, such as company renames, parent-subsidiary relationships, and mismatched countries.

For firms not matched by Revelio’s algorithm, we have an AI agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6) follow this algorithm to construct a candidate match. A second agent then scores the confidence of each proposed match as high, medium, low, or no_match by evaluating the similarity between the firm’s Salesforce name and the LinkedIn page name, whether the country matches, and whether the LinkedIn page has a plausible number of employees. We retain only high- and medium-confidence matches for the final sample.

RCID lookup.

Each matched LinkedIn slug is converted to a Revelio company identifier (RCID) by querying Revelio’s company_mapping table on WRDS, which maps LinkedIn URLs to RCIDs. Of the 2,803 high- and medium-confidence agent matches, 2,679 (96%) yield an RCID, confirming that the matched LinkedIn pages correspond to firms in Revelio’s employment database.

Duplicate resolution.

In some cases, multiple GitHub firms (typically a parent and subsidiary) match to the same LinkedIn page. We identify 82 such duplicate matches that are parent-subsidiary relationships and consolidate them.

URL repair.

A second human reviewer checked, in four batches, the firms whose LinkedIn slugs were dead, redirected, or otherwise inaccessible. The reviewer provided corrected slugs where possible, recovering matches for 46 of 59 firms with broken URLs. This URL repair step corrects link rot but does not independently re-evaluate the agent’s firm identification.

B.5   Match Quality Filters

We apply two pre-launch filters to screen out incorrect links between GitHub and Revelio and to ensure adequate profile coverage among matched firms. First, we exclude matched firms with zero recorded total employment or zero software engineers in Revelio prior to GitHub Copilot’s launch. Second, we exclude matches in which the firm’s average pre-launch total employment in Revelio is smaller than the number of GitHub licenses it purchased. Because each GitHub license corresponds to an individual user license, a firm’s total workforce must be at least as large as its licensed count; violations of this condition indicate either an incorrect entity match or severe profile undercoverage.

These two criteria remove 1,215 matches, leaving 6,959 firms (80% of matched accounts) with verified links and sufficient employment coverage. Excluded accounts are disproportionately public-sector or government organizations, or firms headquartered outside North America and Europe, where online profile coverage is sparser. Because both filters are defined strictly using pre-2023 data prior to GitHub Copilot’s launch, they do not select firms on the basis of subsequent GitHub Copilot adoption or post-launch employment trajectories.

B.6   Validation Sample and Match Accuracy

We evaluate the accuracy of our firm-matching pipeline through three validation exercises. The first two draw random samples of 100 firms from the algorithmic and AI-assisted pipelines, respectively, and compare the assigned match against the company profile page independently identified by a human reviewer using firm name, country, and industry. The third exercise conducts a larger-scale stress test of Revelio’s name-matching algorithm using firms with known ground-truth identifiers.

  1. 1.

    Revelio algorithmic match (precision audit, N = 100). The reviewer compared the Revelio-assigned company (RCID) to the firm they identified independently, recording whether the match was correct, incorrect (wrong firm), or whether no correct match should have existed. Because the audit draws only from firms Revelio matched, it measures precision but not recall.

  2. 2.

    AI agent-assisted match (precision and recall, N = 100). The reviewer compared the agent’s proposed LinkedIn slug to the slug they identified independently. Draws include firms the agent declined to match, so the sample supports both precision and recall.

  3. 3.

    Name-perturbation stress test (N = 995). For 995 firms with known ground-truth RCIDs, we append legal suffixes (e.g., “Ltd.,” “GmbH”) and parent qualifiers (e.g., “ – Parent”) to the firm name before sending it through Revelio’s matching algorithm. This isolates the algorithm’s sensitivity to name-cleanliness variation holding the target firm fixed.

Table A.1 reports precision, recall, and F1 for each test. Revelio’s algorithmic matches are correct for 83 of 100 sampled firms (precision 0.83). The AI agent achieves higher precision (0.93) and near-complete recall (0.99), for an F1 of 0.96: most incorrect cases are firm-level errors (typically a subsidiary matched to its parent), not missed matches. The name-perturbation test yields the same precision (0.93) as the agent pipeline but lower recall (0.76): the algorithm returns no match for 22.7% of perturbed names. This reflects the algorithm’s reliance on exact-match-after-cleaning and motivates the agent-assisted pipeline for firms with non-standard name representations.

Appendix Table A.2 decomposes matching errors into five mutually exclusive categories, each expressed as a percentage of the corresponding validation sample. Assignments to the wrong firm account for the vast majority of errors in the algorithmic audit (16.0% of sampled firms) but fall sharply in the AI-assisted audit (7.0%) and the perturbation test (5.3%). Conversely, missed matches (false negatives) are rare in the AI-assisted audit (1.0%) but account for 22.7% of cases in the perturbation test, confirming that formatting noise primarily causes the rule-based algorithm to leave valid firms unmatched rather than to assign incorrect links.

B.7   Estimation Sample Construction and Summary Statistics

Appendix Table A.3 summarizes the construction of our estimation sample from the universe of pre-existing GitHub accounts. To ensure that scheduled contract review timing is predetermined with respect to GitHub Copilot’s launch, we begin with firms that held an active GitHub contract as of September 2022 with a scheduled post-launch contract review date fixed prior to the introduction of GitHub Copilot. Linking these accounts to Revelio Labs via our algorithmic and AI-assisted matching procedures and applying the pre-launch match-quality filters described in Appendix Section B.5 yields 6,959 matched organizations with verified employment coverage.

From this matched sample, we apply two final sample restrictions. First, we exclude 599 public-sector, government, and nonprofit entities to focus on commercial firms, leaving 6,360 private-sector enterprises.1515 15 We identify public-sector and nonprofit entities using two-digit NAICS code 92 (“Public Administration”), keyword searches for government and non-commercial terms in organization names, and manual verification. Second, to ensure consistent and representative profile coverage across countries, we restrict the sample to firms headquartered in the Americas or Europe, the regions where Revelio’s coverage is most comprehensive.1616 16 Specifically, we retain firms headquartered in six geographic regions classified in Revelio: Northern America, Central America and the Caribbean, Southern America, Northern Europe, Western Europe, and Southern Europe. This restriction excludes 946 firms headquartered in Asia, Africa, the Middle East, or Oceania. The resulting balanced panel comprises 5,414 firms observed monthly from January 2021 through June 2025. Appendix Table A.4 reports September 2022 baseline characteristics for the full sample and by whether firms adopt GitHub Copilot by June 2025.

B.8   Employment Data Validation

Our empirical analysis relies on Revelio Labs data to measure firm-level employment stocks, hiring and separation flows, and workforce composition across technical roles. We validate these measures against two independent external benchmarks: audited total headcount from regulatory filings and administrative records of GitHub Enterprise licenses.

First, for the 19% of sample firms that file Form 10-K reports covered in Compustat, we compare average annual employment in Revelio against total headcount reported in Compustat. The two series differ in several institutional respects: 10-K filings report formal payroll employees at fiscal year-end, whereas Revelio measures annual average active spells based on online profiles, which can include contractors and freelancers. Despite these conceptual differences, the two measures are strongly correlated in log levels (Pearson’s r=0.756r=0.756, Spearman’s ρ=0.705\rho=0.705). More importantly for our longitudinal research design, which relies on within-firm variation over time, year-over-year log employment changes in Revelio and Compustat also track each other closely, with a Pearson correlation of 0.5760.576 and a Spearman rank correlation of 0.5980.598 (0.593 among eventual GitHub Copilot adopters and 0.458 among non-adopters). The first two rows of Appendix Figure A.4 plot these level and growth comparisons.

Second, we validate Revelio’s measurement of technical workforces against firms’ pre-launch GitHub license counts. Administrative license counts and Revelio role headcounts do not map one-to-one: Enterprise contracts often provision licenses in blocks rather than matching exact active headcount, not all software engineers require a license on a given enterprise instance, and firms frequently assign licenses to technical workers in adjacent roles outside core software engineering. Even so, pre-launch GitHub Enterprise licenses and Revelio software engineering headcount exhibit a strong positive correlation in log levels (Pearson’s r=0.684r=0.684). At the median firm, the ratio of licensed GitHub Enterprise licenses to Revelio software engineers is approximately 2.4. When we expand the denominator to include adjacent technical roles that routinely interact with code repositories (specifically, application development, data analytics, quality assurance, and systems and infrastructure engineering), the log-level correlation remains similarly strong (r=0.673r=0.673) and the median ratio of GitHub Enterprise licenses to technical workers is 0.90.9, confirming that Revelio captures the relevant population of technical staff at sample firms. The third row of Appendix Figure A.4 plots these comparisons.

B.9   Coverage of the U.S. Technical Workforce

Although our estimation sample is not representative of the universe of U.S. employers, as GitHub customers are disproportionately large and technology-intensive, these firms account for a substantial share of aggregate U.S. technical employment. As of June 2025, sample firms employ 1,646,968 technical workers in the United States. As an external benchmark, total U.S. employment across the corresponding programming and computing occupations in the Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) is 4,347,980 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), implying that our sample covers approximately 38% of the U.S. programming workforce. Because our estimation sample is restricted to private-sector firms whereas the OEWS benchmark includes both private- and public-sector employment, our sample’s share of private-sector U.S. technical employment is even larger. Appendix Table A.5 reports the national employment counts for each occupation included in the benchmark.

B.10   Code Intensity Prompt

We score each position description once with Claude Sonnet 4.6 at temperature zero. The model sees only the description text, inserted where the prompt reads <position description text>; it does not see the job title, occupation, seniority, employer, location, or date. The prompt below reproduces the prompt’s instructions and the definition of the code-intensity dimension verbatim and the required output format.

⬇
You are scoring the work described in an anonymized job-position description on five dimensions. Score ONLY what the text describes; do not infer from writing style, language, or any place names what kind of person wrote it.
The dimension is a SHARE of the described work, scored as a continuous number in [0, 1]:
[...]
copilot_domain: the share of the described work inside GitHub Copilot’s 2023 capability surface: writing, completing, testing, documenting, explaining, or debugging code (1.0 = all inside; 0.0 = none).
[...]
Position description:
---
<position description text>
---

In Equation (10), the horizon-specific reduced-form coefficient ρ^ℓ\widehat{\rho}_{\ell} is applied to all firms. In Equation (11), the horizon-specific Wald estimate θ^ℓ=ρ^ℓ/π^ℓ\hat{\theta}_{\ell}=\hat{\rho}_{\ell}/\hat{\pi}_{\ell} is applied to adopting firms and multiplied by the complier share of adopters at horizon ℓ\ell, π^ℓ/P^​(Di​ℓ=1)\widehat{\pi}_{\ell}/\widehat{P}(D_{i\ell}=1), where π^ℓ\widehat{\pi}_{\ell} is the first-stage effect and P^​(Di​ℓ=1)\widehat{P}(D_{i\ell}=1) is the sample adoption rate at horizon ℓ\ell. Because adopting firms are larger on average than non-adopters, reweighting the complier effect by adopter hiring levels yields a larger reduction than the unweighted reduced form (3.1 versus 1.7 hires per firm-quarter). In Equation (12), the Wald estimate is applied to all adopting firms without scaling down by the complier share. This assumes that an always taker kk quarters after its own adoption experiences the same proportional hiring effect as a complier kk quarters after its review.
